opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting directions right now, and honestly I'm fairly optimistic about it, though maybe not in the way people usually imagine.

When people say "infinite context," the naive picture is that you just keep stretching the window: 128K, then a million, then ten million tokens. Training at those lengths is extremely expensive, and the data at those lengths is very sparse. There just aren't many natural documents where something at token one really matters for token ten million. So I don't think the path is to train on infinite context directly.

What seems more promising is that the model learns, at a finite length, a set of skills that generalize to much longer horizons at inference time. Things like: how to summarize what it has done so far, how to decide what is worth writing down, how to retrieve from its own past, how to hand off state to a "future self." If a model is really good at managing its own memory within, say, a few hundred thousand tokens, then at inference you can chain those episodes together almost indefinitely. It's a bit like humans. Our working memory is tiny, but we can work on a project for years because we take notes, we organize files, we come back and re-read.

So I'd frame it less as "infinite context" and more as "unbounded horizon with bounded context." That's partly an architecture question, things like linear attention, hybrid models, and compression of the KV cache, but I think more of it is a training and RL question. Do you design tasks where the model is rewarded for keeping good state across many context resets? Agentic coding is a natural testbed, because the tasks are long, the environment persists, and you can verify the outcome.

The hard parts are evaluation and credit assignment. If a model fails at hour ten, was that because of a bad note it wrote at hour one? That's very hard to attribute, and our benchmarks mostly don't measure it yet. Also, length generalization is notoriously brittle. Models that look fine at 2x their training length can degrade in subtle ways at 10x.

So for 2026, my expectation is real progress on the agentic side, models that can work coherently over much longer tasks than their raw window. I'd be more cautious about claims that we've "solved" long context in the pure sense of attending perfectly over millions of tokens. I think the winning recipe will look more like good memory habits than a bigger window.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deciding what is worth writing down and summarizing or retrieving past state, but it does not propose selectively discarding unimportant information to sustain an ongoing personal assistant interaction.

r002.rationale: It presents several possible approaches, but does not locate uncertainty specifically in choosing among technical routes; it emphasizes memory skills, training and RL, and cautious expectations about long context.

r003.rationale: It mentions agentic coding as a testbed and says evaluation is difficult, but does not propose experiments comparing routes by efficiency in typical long-term user scenarios.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most important problems for 2026, and honestly I'd frame it slightly differently: the question isn't really "how long is the context window," it's "how does the model manage its own memory."

Right now we train models on sequences of, say, 128K or a million tokens, and then at inference we ask them to do tasks that span millions or tens of millions of tokens — a multi-day coding agent, or a research task where it reads hundreds of papers. The naive approach is to just keep extending the window. But that runs into two walls. One is cost: attention is quadratic, and even with linear or sparse variants, you're still paying to hold everything. The other is more fundamental — the model never saw sequences that long in training, so its behavior out there is undefined. We've all seen the "lost in the middle" degradation.

So I think the direction that actually works is treating context as a resource the model actively manages, not a passive buffer. If you think about how a human does a long project, we don't keep everything in working memory. We write notes, we build summaries, we decide what to forget, we go back and retrieve when needed. That's the agent paradigm — context becomes an action space. The model learns, through reinforcement learning, when to compress, when to externalize to a file or a scratchpad, when to retrieve. And crucially, you can train that with finite context, because each individual "step" fits in the window — what's unbounded is the number of steps.

The analogy I like is operating systems. Physical RAM is finite, but programs act like they have infinite memory because of virtual memory and paging. The model's context window is RAM. Everything else — tools, files, retrieval, summaries — is disk. The research question is who writes the paging policy. Today it's hand-engineered by whoever builds the agent framework. By the end of 2026 I expect it's increasingly learned end-to-end, because the model knows better than we do what it'll need later.

There's a second piece, which is architectural. I don't think pure transformers are the final answer here. Hybrids with some kind of recurrent or state-space component give you a compressed running state that doesn't grow with sequence length, and then you keep a smaller attention window for precise lookup. Those two complement each other — one is gist, one is detail. We'll see more of that.

The hard part, the thing I'd watch, is evaluation. It's easy to build a benchmark that's a needle-in-a-haystack retrieval test. It's much harder to build one that measures whether a model can sustain a coherent plan across a week of work, notice when its earlier summary was wrong, and correct it. Those long-horizon failure modes are where the real gap is, and right now they're mostly invisible in benchmarks. So my honest prediction for 2026: the engineering will get solved faster than the evaluation does, and we'll have models that look great on paper and still drift on genuinely long tasks. Closing that gap is the interesting work.

r001.rationale: The response says a model should decide what to forget, but does not specify discarding information judged unimportant to sustain an ongoing personal assistant interaction with a user.

r002.rationale: It presents several approaches and makes predictions, but does not identify uncertainty about which technical route to choose as the central issue.

r003.rationale: It calls for better evaluation of week-long task coherence, but does not propose experiments comparing technical routes by efficiency in typical long-term user scenarios.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, but I would separate two questions. One is whether a model can technically accept a context much longer than what it saw during training. The other is whether it can actually use that additional information well. The second question is much harder. Having a million tokens available doesn’t necessarily mean you can connect two important details that are very far apart, or maintain a coherent understanding of everything in between.

For 2026, I’m more optimistic about systems that manage a nearly unlimited history than about a model that directly attends to an unlimited context. An agent can retrieve information, maintain notes, summarize previous interactions, and decide what to bring into its working context. In that setup, finite context becomes a workspace, while external memory can keep growing.

But that also moves the problem: what should you remember, what can you safely compress, and when should you go back to the original information? If you discard something that only becomes relevant later, a longer inference budget won’t recover it unless you preserved a way to find it.

So I think the opportunity is to train models on those operations—reading, writing, retrieving, and revising memory—even within finite training contexts. Then we need to test whether those behaviors remain reliable over much longer interactions. That seems plausible to me, but I wouldn’t assume that scaling the available context alone gives us that capability.

r001.rationale: The response discusses retrieval, notes, summaries, and the risks of discarding useful information, but does not propose selectively discarding information judged unimportant to sustain an ongoing personal-assistant interaction.

r002.rationale: It favors systems that manage history over direct unlimited attention, but does not locate uncertainty in choosing between technical routes; its stated concerns are memory reliability and whether longer context alone is sufficient.

r003.rationale: It calls for testing behaviors over longer interactions, but does not propose comparing technical routes or measuring efficiency in typical long-term user scenarios.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, but I would separate two things: accepting a very long context and actually using it effectively. A model might technically support a million tokens, but that doesn’t mean it can reliably connect information across all of them.

For an agent, you also don’t necessarily want to keep putting its entire history into the prompt. You want it to maintain useful memory, retrieve relevant information, and sometimes go back to the original evidence. So the system can have a potentially unbounded history while the model works with a finite context at each step.

The interesting question is whether we can train those behaviors on shorter tasks and have them generalize to much longer ones. Some things, like finding a particular fact, might generalize fairly well. But a task where you have to accumulate insights over thousands of steps is much harder. Small mistakes in what you remember or discard can compound.

So for 2026, I’m more optimistic about effectively infinite context at the system level than about a single model call that can use arbitrarily long context. And the key metric should be whether the agent keeps making progress as the history grows, rather than simply how many tokens it can take.

r001.rationale: It says an agent should keep useful memory and retrieve relevant information instead of continually placing its entire history in the prompt, implying selective retention for ongoing interaction.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about generalizing training to long tasks and using long context effectively, but does not locate the uncertainty in choosing among technical routes.

r003.rationale: It proposes progress as history grows as a key metric, but does not propose experiments comparing technical routes or measuring efficiency in typical long-term user scenarios.
